To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

storage of tissue sections over 13 weeks is accompanied by a marked decrease in the specific formaldehydefluorescence of monoamine-containing neurons, which can be prevented by mounting the tissue in Entellan.

the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence (FIF) of catecholamines in brain sections is enhanced during storage, and that the enhancement is prevented by mounting sections in Entellan, a plastic mounting medium that also prevents the increase in autofluorecence that occurs during storage of sections.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of formaldehyde fixation, storage of tissue sections, and the use of various mounting media upon the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence derived from monoamine oxidase and upon tissue autofluorescence.

the development of a method for the quantitative histochemical measurement of changes in monoamine levels in the brain during storage of tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intensity of the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence is not a reliable index of the amount of monoamine present in tissue sections.
the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence is a reliable method for the histochemical demonstration of monoamines in tissue sections stored for up to 3 days after fixation.
storage of brain sections in ribbons over a period of several weeks results in a marked increase in both the specific formaldehyde induced fluorescence of monoamines and the autofluorescence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fluorescence intensity of formaldehyde induced fluorescence and autofluoroscence are both affected during storage of tissue section and the changes are dependent on both storage conditions and the tissue.

the fluorescence intensity of formaldehyde induced fluorescence derived from monoamnes and of autofluorescence are affected during storage of tissue in the same way as the fluorescence intensity of the formaldehyde induced fluorescence is affected during storage of formaldehyde induced tissue sections.
the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence is stable for up to 3 days after the tissue sections have been cut and that the autofluorescence increases markedly during the same period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence is a good marker for the storage conditions of tissue sections.

the formaldehyde-induced fluorescence in the striatal neuropils was not due to formaldehyde-induced fluorescence from catecholamines or 5-hydroxytryptamine, but rather was due to the presence of an unknown fluorescent compound.

the fluorescence intensity of formaldehydeinduced specific fluorescence is a function of the time of storage and of the mounting medium used, while the intensity of autofluorescence is a function of time alone.
